Name: belief_persistence_dynamics
Title: Belief Inertia: Measuring and Steering the Update Dynamics of LLM Belief States Under Evidence
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal representation of a belief about a specific item has measurable *inertia*: once a belief state is established (by prior context, first assertion, or parametric prior), the amount of contradicting evidence required to flip it is asymmetric and predictable from an internal 'belief-confidence' direction in activation space. We hypothesize that (a) belief flips occur as an abrupt threshold event in the residual stream rather than gradual, (b) the flip threshold is asymmetric depending on whether new evidence contradicts a first-mentioned claim vs. a parametric prior, and (c) this inertia can be causally reduced/increased by steering along a recoverable 'belief-stability' direction, providing a lever to fix both stubbornness (ignoring evidence) and sycophancy (over-flipping).
Related Work: Suzgun et al. (2025, Nature MI; and 'Belief in the Machine'/KaBLE) establish behaviorally that LLMs conflate belief, knowledge, and fact and show first- vs. third-person asymmetries, but treat belief statically as a one-shot judgment. Knowledge-editing work (MQuAKE) studies whether edited facts propagate but not the dynamics of belief revision under streaming evidence. Sycophancy work (Wang et al.) studies override of knowledge by user pressure but as a static behavior, not as a quantified update threshold. CogConf (2026) models internal confidence for calibration, not belief revision dynamics. NONE characterize belief *update dynamics*: how much accumulating evidence is required to flip an internal belief, the asymmetry (order/anchoring vs. parametric prior), the abrupt-vs-gradual geometry of the flip, or a causal steering lever to tune inertia. We recast the belief-vs-fact problem as a dynamical-systems / hysteresis phenomenon, which is a genuinely new framing.
Abstract: Large language models are known to conflate belief, knowledge, and fact, but existing work treats an LLM's belief about an item as a static one-shot judgment. We instead study belief as a dynamical quantity that must be updated as evidence accumulates, and introduce the notion of belief inertia: the resistance of an internal belief state to revision under contradicting evidence. Using controlled evidence-streaming scenarios (a proposition is first asserted, then increasing amounts of counter-evidence are provided), we track the model's stated belief and its internal belief-confidence representation turn by turn across several open-weight models. We find that (1) belief flips are abrupt threshold events in activation space rather than gradual drifts, exhibiting hysteresis; (2) the flip threshold is strongly asymmetric, with beliefs anchored to a first-mentioned claim or a strong parametric prior requiring substantially more counter-evidence to overturn than newly introduced beliefs; and (3) a linear 'belief-stability' direction, recovered via difference-of-means between pre- and post-flip states, causally controls inertia when added or subtracted from the residual stream, letting us reduce stubbornness or reduce sycophantic over-flipping without harming factual QA. We propose evidence-flip-count and hysteresis-gap as new metrics for belief robustness and show they correlate with downstream failures in updating factual answers. Our results reframe belief-vs-fact confusion as a tunable update-dynamics problem and provide cheap, interpretable interventions. All experiments run on <=9B models feasible for an academic lab.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build evidence-streaming scenarios. Each item = a target proposition P about a specific entity (drawn from factual and neutral/fictional templates). Two regimes: (a) FALSE-prior regime where P contradicts the model's parametric knowledge and evidence supports P; (b) ANCHOR regime where P is first asserted by a source and subsequent turns provide graded counter-evidence (1..k independent contradicting statements). Also a prior-strength axis using well-known vs. obscure facts. ~2-3k items via templating with entity/order randomization and control (no-evidence) conditions. 2) Behavioral dynamics: Query the model's stated belief ('Do you now believe P?') after each evidence turn. Record the evidence-flip-count (turns/statements needed to flip) per condition. Compute asymmetry: flip-count(prior->against) vs. flip-count(against->prior) to quantify hysteresis-gap. Compare across first- vs third-person framings (extending KaBLE's asymmetry finding to dynamics). Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, plus base vs chat pair. 3) Internal geometry: At each evidence turn, extract residual-stream activations at the query position. Train a linear probe for current belief polarity; track probe-decoded belief-confidence trajectory. Test whether the flip is abrupt (sharp sign change / large single-step delta) vs gradual by fitting logistic vs linear trajectories and reporting sharpness. 4) Belief-stability direction: Compute difference-of-means between activations just-before vs just-after flip events to obtain a candidate 'belief-stability' direction; validate with held-out flips. 5) Causal steering: Add/subtract the belief-stability direction and measure change in evidence-flip-count (controllability) and specificity (does factual QA on unrelated items change?). Test both reducing inertia (make stubborn beliefs update faster) and increasing it (reduce sycophantic premature flipping). 6) Downstream link: Correlate per-item inertia/hysteresis with errors on a knowledge-update task (edit-then-query, MQuAKE-style multi-hop). Metrics: evidence-flip-count, hysteresis-gap, flip-sharpness, probe accuracy, steering controllability & specificity, retained factual accuracy (MMLU/TriviaQA subset).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Stated belief may not equal internal belief; we mitigate by pairing behavioral flips with probe-decoded trajectories and reporting divergences. 2) Templated evidence may create surface shortcuts; mitigated by paraphrase/order randomization and control conditions. 3) The belief-stability direction may be nonlinear or example-specific; we test held-out generalization and report negatives as informative. 4) Flip 'abruptness' could be an artifact of discrete querying; we sample fine-grained evidence increments to check. 5) Steering may have off-target effects; specificity and retention metrics quantify this. 6) Effects may vary by model family and prior-strength; we report per-condition rather than universal claims.
